chapter: Chicago union and the Rhythm Kings
title: Failing and then passing the Chicago union exam
summary: Told the union was fixed, he failed his sight-reading exam, got a second chance from secretary Bankard, memorized the intro and passed.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Well, it wasn't easy. See, these fellas, when they came, Rapolo, when he came down here, of course I'm not a well-educated man, I'm not an educated man, and then I was a young man, you know how a young person feels about it like that. Like they say, sometimes he don't even think about danger, he thinks about it after it's too late, you know. But he came down over to the house and he asked me if he'd like me to go to Chicago, join the New Orleans Rhythm Kings. So I told him, I says, well, Rapolo says, you know I'm not in the union. Oh, he says, we got that fixed, Jake. I says, you have? I says, what are you talking about? He says, oh, listen, he says, you don't have to, he says, I understand, you think you've got to go through examination. I says, that's right. You've got to go through an examination in Chicago to pass a union. Oh, he says, well, you've got all that fixed. But I'll be like, yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Finish this? Oh, I think so. We're not in a great hurry. Jake, before we get too far.
Well, you were talking about the union. Yeah. How do you have to finish up that story?

Well, I went off, well, after he came and saw me, he had me convinced that they had everything fixed in the union, that all I had to do was pay my fees and started to work. So, when I went up there, I found out different. They never had anything fixed. I was on my own. So, I went there and reported to the union. They said, well, all right. We'll send you a card for examination. I said, ain't this nice. This is really pretty. But, I figured, like they told me, that they had everything fixed. You see? So, I didn't worry about it. I said, well, if they got everything fixed, I ain't got nothing to worry about. You see? Anything I'll do, it's all right. I went there and reported to the union. I said, well, all right. We'll send you a card for examination. You see? You see? Ain't this nice. This is really pretty. You see? But, I figured, you know, that like they told me, that they had everything fixed. You see? So, I didn't worry about it. I said, well, if they got everything fixed, I ain't got nothing to worry about. You see? Anything I'll do, it's all right. So, I went there and there was about, oh, I would say, because that's a big local, they must have had about 200 people and they're musicians. To be an audience for your...

They just happened to be there, huh? No, to be there for the past examination themselves, you see? I am by myself. You see? New members. I just got in. New members. So, they had a little stand there with four members on there that writes the cards for you. In fact, they were the, what would you call them, the professors or something. If you pass or you don't. Right, they were the judges. The judges. Yeah. And they had a piano there and a professor right there with you. See? They called my name and I took my bass and I went up and the professor started turning the pages on them. A string bass. Now, remember this. At that time, I was playing a three string bass, not a four string bass. Three string bass. So, follow me. I was playing a bass. So, when I went up, the professor at the back, you know, and the instructor said, you know, is that what you play? Three strings on the bass? I said, yes sir. He looked at me, you know. He said, all right. So, he turned to music and says, okay, one, two, three, four. See? So, I'll play it anything. He tapped me. I'll make it short. He tapped me on my shoulder. And he says, listen. He says, I'll tell you what you do. You go back home. He says, you didn't just play that right. I guess they didn't want to tell me that I didn't know how to read and what they were telling the truth. I didn't know a note as big as this bell. So, he said, you go home and he says, when I think you're right, he says, I'll send you another card for examination. So, that was the finale. So, I knew right well that I made a fool out of myself, you see? So, I packed up my bass and going down and I forgot what was the name of the secretary there. Bankard. Bankard. Bankard was the secretary. And he seemed like he took a life into me, you see? When I came down to fly the steps on the half of the flight, see because I was up on the second floor, he says to me, he says, how'd you make it out? And Gus says, not so good. He says, why? I says, well, I'm going to tell you the truth. I says, Mr. Bankard. I can't read or know what I don't know. I know it as big as this building. I said, them fellas fooled me and they told me that everything was, they had everything to fix here. That anything I do, I says, I don't read no music. Oh, he says, no. He says, you can't play a cymbal or anything. I says, well, even at that I would have to know time. I have to know music. He says, well, yeah, that's true too, he says. Well, he says, Abraham, is there anything that I can do to help? He says, let me know and he says, I'll do it, see? So, I thought a while and I says, well, I'll tell you what you do. I says, will you give me another chance and send me your card so I can come back here? He says, but you can't wait. He says, Abraham, what that good that's going to be? He says, that's not going to do you no good if you didn't pass now. He says, in a couple of days you can't pass over again. I says, I think I can do it. Because I took notice, they had about, oh, they must have had about five or six of them before me. And it was only three numbers in that book that the professor was changing, you see? Which I didn't pay, it means they told me everything was fixed, I didn't pay no attention to it, see? I says, I think I can do it. He looked at me and he says, well, he says, I wish I had John Noyiff. He says, you really got courage. He says, but I'll tell you what I'll do. He says, I'll send you a card. So, I says, I'll tell you what you do. Will you do me a favor? He says, what is it? I says, try to put me last as far back as possible. He says, why, Chinky? I says, because I took notice. He says, I told him, I was frank with him. I said, I took notice, there's only three numbers that the professor changes on there in that book. And it's nothing but six, eight temples. I says, there's march temples. Well, I knew that from playing guitar from the professor, you know. He would learn me how to play guitar. I knew the difference between waltzes and fox strats and everything else, you see? Forch temples comes up. He says, well, what is the reason that I think I said? Because I'm going to pay attention with that. And the deductions that they're taking, and I'll be able, I think I'll be able to do it. He looked at me, he says, Chinky. He says, Abraham, because you didn't call me Chinky. There ain't no one would change. He says, Abraham, I'll send you a card. He says, if you've got the nerve enough to come up here, he says, and go over that again. He says, I've got to know the courage to send you another card. I said, well, all right. So, it was about four or five days, and he sent me a card. He did something. So I went up there. And sure enough, he left me way back, you see. But in the meanwhile, there was a few strings that was pulled. Because when they seen that I was jammed and everything else, they introduced me to the hires, you know, to the big shots and things like that, you know. I don't want to mention names. I know their names. But it's no use going through that. So anyway, I went up there in five days. So I kept my ears open with that introduction. Because that's how you play, was the intro. They don't let you play a whole number. Just the introduction to see if you know how to read. Yeah. And I kept that thing right straight in my ears. It was burning my ears, you see. So I took notice of one number that they played. It went, and I'll never forget it.

Yeah. I said, man, I wish I was lucky that he would put that up. Because I had that more insecure than the other two, you see. So I went up there in the car. Boy, it was my rock. He put out that God-dannable. You see what I was doing? And he went, he went, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom. He says, hold on. He says, hey Brian. He says, wasn't you here four or five years ago? I said, yeah, yes sir. He says, well, man, he says, why didn't you do that before? I says, well, I don't know. You're a little excited and nervous. I said, a big audience like this and you say. He says, my boy, he says, you don't understand. He says, in the profession you're in, that's what you're going to need people. You're going to need audience. You've got to have courage. You've got to have spunk to go up there and meet them. He says, if you're going to get nervous, he says, you ain't going to do any good. He says, give the man a call.
Very good. Very good. Very good. Very good.
